# My other projects in detail ## MindBridge: RAG-based student wellbeing chatbot (2026) MindBridge is a chatbot I built to support homesick students. It is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system, built with Python, FAISS, Flan-T5, Groq/Llama and Gradio. I benchmarked a Flan-T5 model against a Groq Llama RAG pipeline to see which gave better, safer answers. I also built a 5-level stress classification system that ranges from mild to severe stress, and it reached a 98% safe-response accuracy rate. # SentinelGuard: my final year project ## The big picture My final year project (FYP) is a smart industrial control system: a zero trust framework for IoT devices, with a focus on reliability. I prefer not to share more detail about the wider project. We are a group of 4 people. The part I'm working on is called SentinelGuard. ## What SentinelGuard is SentinelGuard is an IoT-based automated safety and liquid control system. It monitors the fluid level in physical tanks and automates pump and valve operations in real time. ## How it's built The system is built around an ESP32 microcontroller, relay modules and ultrasonic sensors. The ultrasonic sensors measure how full a tank is, the ESP32 decides what to do, and the relay modules switch the pumps and valves on and off. Data moves over the MQTT protocol, which is lightweight and works well for IoT devices. The system uses custom setpoints, so the operator can choose the levels at which pumps and valves act. It also has fail-safe rules, so that overflows and system failures are prevented even when something goes wrong. Everything is controlled through a custom operator console interface. ## Why reliability matters The goal

That is why SentinelGuard is built with fail-safe rules and automated safety checks instead of relying on manual control. ## Where SentinelGuard fits SentinelGuard is the project's hardware and control side, and it sits inside the larger FYP goal of a zero trust framework for IoT devices.

# My study notes: Operating Systems ## Why I like Operating Systems Operating Systems is my favourite subject so far. I find it fun and interesting, and what I enjoy the most are the algorithms, especially the Banker's algorithm and Round Robin scheduling. ## Round Robin scheduling (my notes) Round Robin is a CPU scheduling algorithm made for time-sharing systems. Every process gets a fixed slice of CPU time called the time quantum. When a process uses up its quantum and is not finished, it goes to the back of the ready queue and the next process gets its turn. This makes it fair, because no process waits forever. The choice of quantum matters. If the quantum is too small, the CPU wastes a lot of time on context switches. If it is too large, Round Robin starts behaving like First Come First Served. ## Banker's algorithm (my notes) The Banker's algorithm is used to avoid deadlock. It is called that because it works like a bank that never lends out more money than it can safely get back. Before granting a resource request, the system checks whether it would still be in a safe state. A safe state means

out more money than it can safely get back. Before granting a resource request, the system checks whether it would still be in a safe state. A safe state means there is some order in which all processes can finish with the resources available. The algorithm keeps track of the Available resources, each process's Max demand and its current Allocation. The remaining Need is Max minus Allocation. If granting the request leaves the system safe, the request is approved. If not, the process has to wait. ## Why these two algorithms I like them because they are logical and step by step. You can work through an example on paper and see exactly why a decision was made. That is why OS feels interesting to me and not just theory.
